dct_description_sm: This research documents and mobilizes Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit (IQ) and ecological knowledge to better understand common eider harvesting, stewardship, and population dynamics in the context of climate change and food security. The study is conducted in partnership with the community of Kinngait, Nunavut, the Aiviq Hunters and Trappers Organization (HTO) and the Nunavut Wildlife Management Board (NWMB). The research explores three interconnected themes: (1) the socioeconomic and food security dimensions of eider harvesting; (2) Inuit stewardship principles, particularly Avatittinnik Kamatsiarniq (care and respect for land and animals), as a foundation for eider management; and (3) Inuit knowledge of long-term changes in eider abundance and distribution in Hudson Strait. Data are gathered using community-based and participatory approaches grounded in Indigenous and decolonizing methodologies, including the Aajiiqatigiingniq Inuit research methodology. Methods include cost-of-harvest surveys, GIS tracking of travel routes and harvesting activities, interviews with harvesters and Elders, participatory mapping, storytelling, land-based participant observation, and collaborative workshops. Historical and contemporary knowledge related to the cultural and socioeconomic importance of eider to Kinngarmiut is recorded through interviews, participatory mapping, workshops and land-based eider harvesting activities. Eider harvesters document current harvesting patterns through an app-based GIS platform. Knowledge holders retain ownership of the knowledge they share. Ecological data and IQ are then synthesized using innovative social-ecological modelling approaches, including fuzzy cognitive mapping, joint species distribution models, and agent-based simulations. These models examine relationships among harvesters, eiders, and polar bears, and project how harvesting, species distributions, and humanwildlife interactions may shift under climate change scenarios. The data will be used to co-develop an eider stewardship plan, assess changes in harvest costs and food security, and generate community-relevant social-ecological scenarios. Results will support local and regional wildlife co-management, identify emerging challenges and opportunities for sustaining harvests, and inform decision-making related to food security, eider conservation, and climate adaptation. Findings will be validated and shared with community partners to ensure relevance and accessibility.
